blocks.text: Plants are distributed in different habitats of aquatic, moderate, severely dry terrestrial and saline nature, thus termed as hydrophytes, mesophytes, xerophytes and halophytes, respectively.

Hydrophytes are adapted to aquatic environments, including marine and freshwater ecosystems, through specialized osmotic adjustment mechanisms. Marine hydrophytes thrive in saline (hypertonic) conditions, where water tends to leave their cells. They excrete excess salts using specialized salt glands and synthesize organic solutes like proline, glycine betaine, and sugars to retain water by increasing their internal osmotic potential. They have thick cuticles which further reduce water loss, and they exhibit halophytic traits to tolerate high salinity. Freshwater hydrophytes grow in hypotonic environments, where water continuously enters their cells. These plants expel excess water through structures like hydathodes or vacuoles to avoid overhydration. They actively absorb essential ions, such as potassium and calcium, to maintain osmotic balance and compensate for the dilute surroundings. With thin or absent cuticles, these plants facilitate water exchange and often have reduced root systems, relying on direct nutrient and water absorption from their environment. Examples of hydrophytes are water lilies, lotus, seaweeds and tape grass (Fig. 8.17).

blocks.alt: Two pictures side by side. (a) Water lilies: round, notched leaves floating close together on dark water, with two open white flowers and white buds. (b) Tape grass: long, ribbon-like green leaves rising from the bed of a freshwater lake into blue-green water.
blocks.caption: Figure 8.17: (a) Waterlily floating in freshwater. (b) Tape grass in freshwater lake (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 8.17).

blocks.text: Mesophytes live in moderate environments that are neither too dry nor too wet. They prefer soil that is not waterlogged and has a moderate salt content and humidity. Mesophytes have well-developed roots and shoots with a fully formed vascular system. They do not require any special adaptations to survive. Their leaves are flat, broad, and green with stomata on the surface. Examples of mesophytes include rose, tomatoes, and daisies (Fig.8.18).

blocks.alt: Two pictures side by side. Left: a pink-red rose in full bloom with closed red buds on green stems behind it. Right: a field of white daisies with yellow centres among green stems.
blocks.caption: Figure 8.18: Examples of mesophytes, left (rose) and right (daisy) (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 8.18).

blocks.text: Xerophytes are plants that are adapted to survive in dry conditions. They have special adaptations to minimize water loss and store water. Plants that store water are known as succulents. They possess fleshy stems that can store water and used when needed. Other adaptations in xerophytes include waxy coatings on leaves to reduce water loss, leaf dropping during dry periods, and leaf folding or repositioning to absorb sunlight efficiently. Examples of xerophytes include thorn trees, desert marigold, and blue agave (Fig. 8.19).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In xerophytes, rolling or folding the leaves and turning them edge-on to the sun reduce the light and heat a leaf receives. The purpose is less sunlight, not better absorption: leaf folding or repositioning reduces exposure to sunlight and so reduces water loss.

blocks.alt: A desert under a blue sky. A tall cactus with upturned arms stands on the left; behind it is a flat-topped, orange-red rocky hill; low desert shrubs and small cacti grow in the foreground.
blocks.caption: Figure 8.19: A xerophytic plant (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 8.19).

blocks.text: Halophytes inhabit saline soil with high concentrations of salts like NaCl, MgCl₂, MgSO₄, or saline water. On such a substratum, only such plants can grow which can tolerate a relatively high concentration of these salts. These plants have succulent leaves and sometimes the stem is also succulent. In certain cases, leaves are modified into spines. Examples of halophytes are sea arrowgrass and sea lavender.

blocks.alt: A clump of sea arrowgrass on a muddy shore: many narrow, grass-like leaves spread from one base, with slender upright flower spikes bearing small brownish flowers. Behind it are calm grey-blue water and a far bank of green reeds under a pale sky.
blocks.caption: Figure 8.20: Sea Arrowgrass (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 8.20).

blocks.text: Halophytes growing in marshy places near seashore form a special vegetation known as the mangrove or tidal woodland. These are also called Helophilous halophytes.
